title_en: China Life Insurance Company, Chengdu Branch v. Hualong Company, et al. — dispute over securities infringement
ruling_gist_en: After a securities brokerage handles designated transactions and revocation of designated transactions for a client in accordance with regulations, the result that the treasury bond funds in the client's securities account have been cashed and used by the fund user shall be deemed to be in line with the client's intention, and there is no necessary causal relationship with the securities brokerage's act of handling designated transactions and revoking designated transactions.
keywords_en: Civil; Securities infringement dispute; Second instance; Supreme People's Court; Sichuan Province; Chongqing Municipality; Legal person; Financial institution; General Principles of the Civil Law; Whether there is a causal relationship between the securities brokerage's act of handling designated transactions and revoking designated transactions and the fund loss; Whether a third party should bear joint and several liability; Partially upheld; Securities designated transaction; Realization of treasury bond funds; Account linking; Entrusted asset management; Securities; Securities infringement dispute suing Hualong Company et al.
full_text_en:
China Life Insurance Company Chengdu Branch v. Hualong Company et al. — Dispute over Securities Tort

【Ruling Summary】

After a securities business department handles the designation of trading and cancellation of designation of trading for a client in accordance with regulations, if the treasury bond funds in the client's securities account are realized and used by a capital user, it shall be determined that this is consistent with the client's intention, and there is no necessary causal relationship between this result and the business department's handling of the designation and cancellation of designation of trading.

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court

(2004) Min Er Zhong Zi No. 137

Appellant (Plaintiff at first instance): China Life Insurance Company Chengdu Branch, domiciled at No. 58 Jinli East Road, Chengdu City, Sichuan Province.

Person in charge: Qing Derong, General Manager of the branch.

Agent ad litem: Gao Yue, attorney at Beijing King & Wood Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Yuan Jiyu, attorney at Shanghai Haohua Law Firm.

Appellant (Third party at first instance): Dapeng Securities Co., Ltd. Chengdu Luoguoxiang Securities Business Department, domiciled at No. 25 Luoguoxiang, Chengdu City, Sichuan Province.

Person in charge: Jiang Xingjie, General Manager of the business department.

Agent ad litem: Gu Peidong, attorney at Sichuan Kangwei Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Fan Bin, attorney at Sichuan Kangwei Law Firm.

Original Defendant: Sichuan Hualong Investment Consulting Co., Ltd., domiciled at No. 27 Consulate Road, Chengdu City, Sichuan Province.

Legal Representative: Deng Yong, General Manager of the company.

Original Third Party: Dapeng Securities Co., Ltd. Chongqing Shanxi Road Securities Trading Business Department, domiciled at 6th Floor, Xiexin Commercial Building, No. 33 Shanxi Road, Yuzhong District, Chongqing City.

Person in charge: Zhong Jian, General Manager of the business department.

Agent ad litem: Gu Peidong, attorney at Sichuan Kangwei Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Fan Bin, attorney at Sichuan Kangwei Law Firm.

For the dispute over securities tort with the original defendant Sichuan Hualong Investment Consulting Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Hualong Company) and the original third party Dapeng Securities Co., Ltd. Chongqing Shanxi Road Securities Trading Business Department (hereinafter referred to as Chongqing Dapeng), the appellant China Life Insurance Company Chengdu Branch (hereinafter referred to as Zhongbao Life) and the appellant Dapeng Securities Co., Ltd. Chengdu Luoguoxiang Securities Business Department (hereinafter referred to as Chengdu Dapeng) appealed against the civil judgment (2003) Chuan Min Chu Zi No. 22 rendered by the Sichuan High People's Court, and filed an appeal with this Court. This Court formed a collegial panel according to law, with trial judge Wu Qingbao presiding, and acting judges Gong Bangyou and Liu Min participating in the deliberation, and court clerk Kong Ling serving as recorder. The case has now been concluded.

The facts found by the original trial court are as follows:

On March 22, 1999, Zhongbao Life sent its employee Xiang Hua to Chengdu Dapeng to handle the procedures for entrustment and designation of trading (Shanghai shareholder code: B880217601, Shenzhen shareholder code: 79035484, fund account: 791293), and set a password for account B880217601. On April 1, 1999, Zhongbao Life cancelled the designation of trading of account B880217601 at Chengdu Dapeng. On July 26, 1999, Zhongbao Life transferred RMB 40 million to Chengdu Dapeng via bank transfer. On July 28, 1999, account B880311617 (hereinafter referred to as account 617) of Hualong Company was linked to Zhongbao Life's fund account 791293. From July 29, 1999 to August 2, 1999, Chengdu Dapeng used account 617 to subscribe for 000896 treasury bonds with the entire RMB 40 million. On August 10, 1999, Zhongbao Life applied to cancel the Shanghai A-share account 791293. Chengdu Dapeng cancelled account 617. On the same day, account 617 was designated by Hualong Company to Xiamen Securities Co., Ltd. Chengdu Xinghui Road Securities Business Department (hereinafter referred to as Xiamen Securities).

On August 13, 1999, Lei Shaocheng handled the designation of trading at Xiamen Securities. On August 15, 1999, Hualong Company issued a letter of commitment to Xiamen Securities: "Our company agrees to link our company's securities (account name: Sichuan Hualong Investment Company, Shanghai account: 617, Shenzhen account: 34795671) as a sub-account under the account of Lei Shaocheng (Shanghai account: A307515423, Shenzhen account: 54441491), and undertakes to bear all related civil and legal liabilities. This matter is hereby entrusted to Mr. Deng Yong of our company for handling." Thereafter, Lei Shaocheng sold all the 000896 treasury bonds in account 617 and used the funds for stock trading in his own account. On March 14, 2000, Hualong Company transferred 525,520 lots of stock code 0682 from Lei Shaocheng's account to Huaxia Securities Majia Huayuan Securities Business Department (hereinafter referred to as Huaxia Securities) (seat number: 205800). From 1999 to 2001, over three years, three payments totaling RMB 18,412,560 (each RMB 6,137,520) were transferred from Lei Shaocheng's account at Xiamen Securities and Chen Daopu's account at Huaxia Securities to Zhongbao Life's account 791293 at Chengdu Dapeng, and were then transferred back by Zhongbao Life to the company.

On August 24, 1999 and December 24, 1999, RMB 2.08 million and RMB 2.8 million were respectively transferred from Lei Shaocheng's account at Xiamen Securities to Zhongbao Life's account at the Ren South Sub-branch of Chengdu No. 1 Construction Bank.

On October 17, 1999, Zhongbao Life and Chongqing Dapeng signed an "Asset Custody and Management Agreement", stipulating: Zhongbao Life entrusts Chongqing Dapeng with the custody and management of 71,700 lots of treasury bonds code 000896; Zhongbao Life shall, within five working days after the signing of this agreement, authorize the transfer of the negotiable treasury bonds to Chongqing Dapeng for management; the management period shall be from the date Zhongbao Life authorizes and transfers the negotiable securities to Chongqing Dapeng to October 30, 2003; Zhongbao Life shall pay Chongqing Dapeng a lump sum treasury bond income of RMB 4.88 million, to be paid in full before December 31, 1999. Zhongbao Life and Chongqing Dapeng affixed their seals to the agreement, and Zhang Zhiyong, General Manager of Chongqing Dapeng, signed the agreement.

In March 2002, Chongqing Dapeng issued a letter of commitment to Zhongbao Life: "At your request, our department agrees in principle to terminate the 'Treasury Bond Custody and Management Contract' one year early, i.e., our department agrees to sell the treasury bonds (000896) 71,700 lots before October 31, 2002, and settle the funds based on the average price of the week (5 trading days) before payment, i.e., the average closing price of October 24, 25, 28, 29, and 30, and transfer the settlement funds to your designated bank account before October 31." Chongqing Dapeng affixed its seal to the commitment letter. Because Zhongbao Life did not receive the treasury bond interest for 2002, it discovered that Chengdu Dapeng had not purchased RMB 40 million worth of treasury bonds for its account B880217601, and thus filed a lawsuit with the Sichuan High People's Court. Zhongbao Life believed that Hualong Company, without its consent, misappropriated the funds in its account, constituting a tort, and should return the funds and bear the resulting losses. The third party Chengdu Dapeng, by violating operational rules and deceiving Zhongbao Life, was an important reason for Hualong Company's tort, and should bear joint and several liability. The third party Chongqing Dapeng, despite knowing that the treasury bond custody and management agreement signed with Zhongbao Life had not been performed, used methods such as paying interest and issuing a letter of commitment to conceal Hualong Company's tort, which was one of the reasons enabling Hualong Company's tort to continue, and should also bear joint and several liability for Hualong Company's tort results. Therefore, the claims were: 1. Order Hualong Company to return RMB 40 million and corresponding losses; 2. Order the two third parties to bear joint and several liability for the first claim; 3. The litigation costs of this case to be borne by Hualong Company and the two third parties jointly.

It was also found that Zhang Zhiyong was removed from the position of General Manager of Chongqing Dapeng by Dapeng Securities Co., Ltd. on February 23, 2001. He was arrested by the Chongqing Public Security Bureau in January 2002 and is currently detained in the Chongqing Detention Center.

Furthermore, RMB 6,137,520 was the one-year interest on RMB 90 million of treasury bonds. During the trial, the original trial court, upon the application of Zhongbao Life, preserved evidence regarding the account opening and related transaction materials of Zhongbao Life and Chengdu Dapeng at Chengdu Dapeng.

The original trial court, upon the application of Chengdu Dapeng, ex officio obtained the following evidence: 1. The reply letter from the Information Center of the Shanghai Stock Exchange; 2. The designation of trading agreement of Xiamen Securities client Lei Shaocheng; the commitment letter of Hualong Company; the special withdrawal slip for funds of Xiamen Securities; the power of attorney; the transfer custody application; 3. The interrogation record of Zhang Zhiyong by the original trial court; 4. The inquiry record of Xiang Hua by the original trial court. After the original trial court organized the parties to cross-examine, Zhongbao Life did not dispute the authenticity of the evidence collected by the original trial court, but argued that the interrogation record of Zhang Zhiyong was hearsay evidence and circumstantial evidence.

The Sichuan High People's Court held that the focus of this case was: 1. Whether the actions of Hualong Company constituted a tort; 2. Whether Chengdu Dapeng should bear liability in this case; 3. Whether Chongqing Dapeng should bear liability in this case.

Hualong Company, without any authorization from Zhongbao Life, unlawfully used Zhongbao Life's treasury bonds, causing Zhongbao Life's funds to be irrecoverable. Its actions constituted a tort against Zhongbao Life and should bear liability for compensation for the losses caused to Zhongbao Life.

On March 22, 1999, Zhongbao Life opened an account with Chengdu Dapeng and signed a designation agreement (account B880217601), which was the true intention of both parties, did not violate relevant national laws and regulations, and was valid. The cancellation of the Shanghai stock designation of trading by Zhongbao Life from Chengdu Dapeng on April 1 of the same year was also valid. Regarding the designation of trading agreement (account 617) submitted to the court by the third party Chengdu Dapeng, dated March 22, 1999, between Zhongbao Life and Chengdu Dapeng, the securities account of Party A on it had been changed from A79035484 to 617. Zhongbao Life did not recognize this evidence. Since this evidence had been held by Chengdu Dapeng, and Chengdu Dapeng could not explain to the court the reason for the added handwriting on this evidence, the court did not admit this evidence. As for the Application for (Fund/Transaction Account) Addition/Password Change dated July 28, 1999, Chengdu Dapeng argued that because the words "fund" and "password change" on the application had been crossed out, it was used by Zhongbao Life to link an account and was a transaction account addition application. However, Zhongbao Life denied that the handwriting for linking account 617 on the application was written by its handler Xiang Hua; and argued that the crossing out of "fund" and "password change" was done unilaterally by the third party Chengdu Dapeng. The court held that the form used for this evidence was the Application for (Fund/Transaction Account) Addition/Password Change. The words "fund" and "password change" in the evidence had been crossed out. The third party Chengdu Dapeng claimed that this proved Zhongbao Life had applied to link a sub-account under its fund account. The prerequisite for this claim to stand was that the third party Chengdu Dapeng should prove that the alteration was done jointly by both parties or before the seal of Zhongbao Life was affixed, but Chengdu Dapeng failed to provide evidence to prove this. Therefore, this evidence could not prove that linking Hualong Company's account was done based on Zhongbao Life's application. Zhongbao Life denied that the content in the form was written by its handler Xiang Hua, but did not deny the authenticity of the official seal affixed to the application. Therefore, except for the altered part, the rest of the content of this evidence was admitted by the court. Since Zhongbao Life did not apply to the court for a handwriting examination of this evidence, and the application bore the official seal of Zhongbao Life, Zhongbao Life's argument that this evidence was used for changing the password and that the handwriting was made by Chengdu Dapeng was insufficiently evidenced. This application should be regarded as an act of Zhongbao Life.

Regarding the cancellation of designation of trading application dated August 10, 1999, because the application (counterfoil copy) submitted by the third party Chengdu Dapeng had the words "617" added after 791293, which was inconsistent with the copy (customer copy) submitted by Zhongbao Life to the court, and the handler Xiang Hua of Zhongbao Life stated to the court that the handwriting was not his. According to Article 75 of the Supreme People's Court's "Provisions on Evidence in Civil Proceedings": "If both parties present contrary evidence on the same fact, but neither has sufficient grounds to negate the other's evidence, the people's court shall, in light of the circumstances of the case, determine whether the probative force of one party's evidence is significantly greater than that of the other party's evidence, and confirm the evidence with greater probative force. If it is difficult to determine the disputed fact due to the inability to judge the probative force of the evidence, the people's court shall make a ruling according to the rules on the allocation of the burden of proof." Since the third party Chengdu Dapeng did not have sufficient evidence to prove that the added handwriting on the application dated August 10, 1999 was made by Zhongbao Life, the court accordingly determined that the added handwriting on the cancellation of designation of trading application was made by the third party Chengdu Dapeng and was not the true intention of Zhongbao Life. The third party Chengdu Dapeng, without authorization, added handwriting to Zhongbao Life's application, causing Zhongbao Life's stocks to be transferred away by Hualong Company and thereby losing control over them. Its illegal conduct objectively caused the insecurity of Zhongbao Life's funds. Therefore, Chengdu Dapeng should bear supplementary compensation liability for Zhongbao Life's losses. Since Zhongbao Life had already received the three-year treasury bond interest from 1999 to 2001 totaling RMB 18,412,560 for RMB 90 million, which included the interest for the RMB 40 million in this case, the interest in this case should be calculated from January 1, 2002, at the one-year demand deposit interest rate of the People's Bank of China.

Since Zhongbao Life also failed to exercise sufficient duty of care in this case, according to Article 131 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China: "If the victim is also at fault for the occurrence of the damage, the civil liability of the injuring party may be reduced." Zhongbao Life should also bear 10% of the liability for the losses incurred. The corresponding portion of the RMB 4.88 million income received by Zhongbao Life attributable to the RMB 40 million, i.e., RMB 2,168,888.89, should be offset against the principal.

Chongqing Dapeng, despite not having received the treasury bonds from Zhongbao Life, signed a false asset custody and management agreement with Zhongbao Life and promised to repay the treasury bonds and interest. Chongqing Dapeng argued that this act was a personal act of Zhang Zhiyong, and that both the agreement and the commitment letter were forged by Zhang Zhiyong, but did not deny the authenticity of the official seal of Chongqing Dapeng on the agreement and commitment letter. The court held that, at the time of signing the agreement with Zhongbao Life, the treasury bonds of Zhongbao Life at Chengdu Dapeng had already been designated by Hualong Company to Xiamen Securities and sold. Zhongbao Life had not actually delivered the 000896 treasury bonds as stipulated in the agreement to Chongqing Dapeng, and the RMB 4.88 million income was not directly paid by Chongqing Dapeng. Therefore, this agreement should be regarded as not having been actually performed. Since the third party did not apply to the court for an authenticity examination of the agreement, the third party Chongqing Dapeng's argument that the agreement was forged could not be sustained. Regarding the commitment letter issued by Chongqing Dapeng to Zhongbao Life in March 2002, the court held that, at the time Chongqing Dapeng issued the commitment letter, Zhongbao Life's funds had already been occupied by Hualong Company. Therefore, there was no direct causal relationship between this commitment letter and the economic losses suffered by Zhongbao Life. Chongqing Dapeng should not bear liability for Zhongbao Life's losses. As for other disputes between Chongqing Dapeng and Zhongbao Life, they should be handled in separate proceedings. Chongqing Dapeng's defense was well-founded.

In summary, part of Zhongbao Life's claims were sustained. In accordance with Articles 128 and 130 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, Articles 117(1)(3) and 131 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 145 of the Securities Law of the People's Republic of China, and after discussion by the Adjudication Committee of this court, the judgment is as follows:

1. Hualong Company shall, within ten days from the effective date of this judgment, return RMB 37,831,111.11 to Zhongbao Life, together with corresponding interest (calculated from January 1, 2002 to the date of full payment at the one-year demand deposit interest rate of the People's Bank of China);

2. Chengdu Dapeng shall bear supplementary compensation liability for 90% of the above amount of RMB 37,831,111.11 and interest;

Court acceptance fee for this case: RMB 252,010, to be borne by Hualong Company in the amount of RMB 126,005, by the third party Chengdu Dapeng in the amount of RMB 75,603, by the third party Chongqing Dapeng in the amount of RMB 25,201, and by Zhongbao Life in the amount of RMB 25,201.

Chengdu Dapeng, dissatisfied with the aforementioned civil judgment of the Sichuan High People's Court, appealed to this Court, alleging: First, on December 29, 1999, Hualong Company transferred RMB 6,137,520 from Lei Shaocheng's fund account at Xiamen Securities to the appellee's fund account 791293; on November 3, 2000, Hualong Company transferred RMB 6,137,520 from Chen Daopu's fund account at Huaxia Securities, which it controlled, to the appellee's fund account 791293. As found by the court of first instance, RMB 6,137,520 constituted the one-year interest on the total RMB 90 million in treasury bonds, including the disputed RMB 40 million and the RMB 50 million which the appellee admitted it had transferred on its own. Second, the record of the court of first instance's interrogation of Zhang Zhiyong indicated that there existed a financing relationship of RMB 90 million between the appellee and Hualong Company, and that the person in charge of the appellee was fully aware of this. The appellee and Hualong Company adopted a method whereby the appellee purchased treasury bonds and the Hualong Company's securities account was subordinated under the fund account, thereby channeling the appellee's funds to Hualong Company for stock trading, with Hualong Company paying financing interest to the appellee. The disputed RMB 40 million, like the first tranche of RMB 50 million, was an illegal interbank lending between the appellee and Hualong Company. The Application for Adding Trading Account dated July 28, 1999, represented the appellee's true intention. Third, the judgment of first instance found that the revocation of the designated trading of securities account No. 617 on August 10, 1999, was not the appellee's true intention; this finding violated evidentiary rules and contradicted objective facts. The appellee's purpose in completing the Application for Revocation of Designated Trading was to revoke the designated trading of the Shanghai A-share securities account under fund account 791293. Regardless of whether "617" after "Securities Account: Shanghai A-share 791293" was added later or by whom, it does not affect the appellee's purpose when completing the application form. Thus, revoking the designated trading of the Shanghai securities account (necessarily account 617) under fund account 791293 was the appellee's true intention, and the transfer of the treasury bonds therein was the appellee's own act. The appellee's inability to recover the treasury bond funds resulted from its own actions and was unrelated to the appellant. In summary, the actual transactions of the RMB 40 million in funds and interest in this case occurred solely between the appellee and Hualong Company; there existed an illegal interbank lending relationship between them. The illegal interbank lending between the appellee and Hualong Company was unrelated to the appellant, and the consequence of the appellee's inability to recover the loaned funds should be borne by the appellee itself. The court of first instance made significant errors in its overall approach to the case, and also committed obvious mistakes in its specific findings regarding the Application for Adding Trading Account and the Application for Revocation of Designated Trading. All transactions and fund transfers involving the appellee's fund account and its subordinated securities accounts in this case were conducted by the appellee. The appellant faithfully executed all instructions of the appellee in this case and was not at fault. It requested the Supreme People's Court to ascertain the facts in accordance with the law and uphold its appeal seeking exemption from liability.

Zhongbao Life also, dissatisfied with the original judgment, appealed to this Court, alleging: First, the court of first instance correctly found that, in the "Designated Trading Agreement" of March 22, 1999, the securities account of Party A was changed from A79035484 to account 617; and correctly found that the addition of the words "made by third party Chengdu Dapeng" on the revocation of designated trading document dated August 10, 1999, was also correct. However, there were issues with its finding on the "Application for Adding/Modifying Password (for Fund/Trading Account)" dated July 28, 1999. The appellant submitted this application to add or modify the password for the Hualong Company's securities account subordinated under its own fund account. But considering the facts of the entire case, the appellant never knew of Hualong Company's existence and had no intention or act to subordinate account 617. How could there be an isolated issue of adding or modifying the password for account 617? Therefore, this finding lacks supporting evidence and cannot stand. Second, pursuant to Article 75 of the Supreme People's Court's Several Provisions on Evidence in Civil Litigation, and in light of the relevant evidence, the logical conclusion should be that Chengdu Dapeng used the blank application form (which the appellant had stamped and intended to be used solely for confirming the trading password for its own Shenzhen securities account) for adding or modifying passwords, to create a false appearance of legality for the unauthorized use of the appellant's funds through account 617. This act constituted one of the false documents it fabricated in the course of assisting Hualong Company in its infringement. Third, Chengdu Dapeng should bear joint and several compensatory liability with Hualong Company, rather than being liable for a proportional supplemental compensation with the appellant. In the judgment of first instance, the finding that Chengdu Dapeng was at fault was correct, but the liability imposed on it was inappropriate. Chengdu Dapeng and Hualong Company objectively engaged in joint tortious conduct, causing damage to the appellant. First, the actions of Chengdu Dapeng and Hualong Company formed an integrated whole, which together caused the appellant's losses. For Hualong Company to unlawfully occupy the appellant's funds and transfer the purchased treasury bonds, it required complete assistance from Chengdu Dapeng. In fact, Chengdu Dapeng carried out a series of assisting acts that Hualong Company needed. Without Chengdu Dapeng's assistance and support, Hualong Company's actions could not have succeeded. Second, the actions of both Chengdu Dapeng and Hualong Company were illegal and in violation of regulations. Chengdu Dapeng and Hualong Company shared subjective fault. They should bear joint and several compensatory liability for the resulting damage. The judgment of first instance found that the appellant "failed to exercise sufficient duty of care" in this case, and then, pursuant to Article 131 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the PRC, held that the appellant itself should bear 10% of the loss. This finding was specious. The precondition for applying Article 131 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the PRC is that both the tortfeasor and the victim contributed to the fault, and that these faults were causally related to the damage. The current judgment effectively found that the appellant "failed to exercise sufficient duty of care." Fourth, while Chongqing Dapeng did not actually manage the appellant's treasury bonds, it consistently diverted the appellant's attention and interfered with the appellant's vigilance through actions such as paying interest and issuing letters of commitment. Its conduct was intentional and served to conceal Hualong Company's infringement. From this, it can be inferred that Chongqing Dapeng acted in malicious collusion with Hualong Company; at a minimum, its conduct constituted subsequent aiding acts in furtherance of Hualong Company's infringement, and prior collusion cannot be ruled out. It was precisely because of Chongqing Dapeng's conduct that the appellant was unable to timely exercise its right of recourse to recover its losses. Therefore, Chongqing Dapeng and Hualong Company also constituted joint tortfeasors and should, according to law, bear joint and several liability with Hualong Company. In summary, both Chengdu Dapeng and Chongqing Dapeng in this case should bear joint and several compensatory liability with Hualong Company. The second holding of the first instance judgment and the ruling on the allocation of litigation costs should be corrected. The appellant's second and third requests in the first instance should be upheld. We implore the Supreme People's Court to support the appellant's appeal in accordance with the law.

Chongqing Dapeng submitted its statement: First, the Asset Entrusted Management Agreement was not performed. Zhongbao Life admitted in its complaint: "Without the actual delivery of securities by our side...", thus, both parties do not dispute that the agreement was not actually performed. Second, Zhongbao Life knew at the time of signing the agreement that it could not be performed. The date on the agreement indicates it was signed in November 1999, but during the second instance, our side provided evidence proving that Zhongbao Life knew as early as June 17, 1999, that RMB 50 million of the treasury bonds no longer existed. Therefore, Zhongbao Life knew at the time of signing that the agreement was impossible to perform. Hence, when signing the agreement, Zhongbao Life either intended to deceive Chongqing Dapeng or had some other illegal purpose. When filing its lawsuit, Zhongbao Life did not name Chongqing Dapeng as a defendant (only as a third party) and did not allege that Chongqing Dapeng had misappropriated RMB 90 million in treasury bonds. This demonstrates that Zhongbao Life knew the agreement and the letter of commitment were false. Otherwise, Chongqing Dapeng would have been named a defendant, not a third party. Third, neither the interest nor the RMB 4.88 million in proceeds were paid by Chongqing Dapeng. The court of first instance found that the interest came from Hualong Company, and the transfer receipts prove that Zhongbao Life knew the funds were paid from the accounts of Lei Shaocheng and Chen Daopu, not from Chongqing Dapeng. Zhongbao Life also failed to provide evidence that these funds were paid by Chongqing Dapeng through Lei Shaocheng or Chen Daopu. Fourth, there is no direct causal link between the Letter of Commitment and Zhongbao Life's financial losses. The date on the Letter of Commitment indicates it was issued in March 2002. However, the objective fact is that by that time, treasury bond 000896 did not exist at all, so the premise for the commitment was not established. Moreover, Zhongbao Life's alleged financial losses already existed before the Letter of Commitment was issued and are not necessarily related to whether the Letter of Commitment was issued. Fifth, Zhongbao Life was not deceived by the agreement or the Letter of Commitment. Our side presented substantial evidence during court proceedings to prove that there was a financing relationship between Zhongbao Life and Hualong Company, that the RMB 40 million in funds was also used by Zhongbao Life itself to purchase the corresponding treasury bonds into Hualong Company's account 617, and that there was no misappropriation of the RMB 40 million in this case. Additionally, Zhang Zhiyong's testimony fully reflects that the "Agreement" and "Letter of Commitment" were privately forged by Zhongbao Life and Deng Yong using pre-stamped blank documents, without his approval and certainly without Chongqing Dapeng's approval. The Letter of Commitment also states that it was issued "at the request of your company." In fact, the purpose of Zhongbao Life and Deng Yong forging these two documents was to conceal the true financing arrangement between Zhongbao Life and Deng Yong, to cope with inspections by their superior companies, and to shift the risk to Chongqing Dapeng in case Deng Yong was unable to repay. Sixth, this case should not be characterized as a tort dispute but as a general creditor-debt dispute. The evidence shows that the RMB 40 million belonging to Zhongbao Life was not misappropriated; rather, Zhongbao Life itself used it to purchase treasury bonds. Therefore, this case is a general debt dispute between Zhongbao Life and Hualong Company, not a tort dispute. Chongqing Dapeng had no actual connection to the RMB 40 million or the treasury bonds and should not have been made a third party in this case. In summary, first, the Asset Entrusted Management Agreement is false, impossible to perform, and was indeed not performed. Chongqing Dapeng should not bear contractual obligations. Second, Chongqing Dapeng was not at all involved in Zhongbao Life's purchase of treasury bonds or receipt of interest, and has no legal connection to this case. It should not have been named a third party. Third, the agreement and the letter of commitment were forged by Zhongbao Life and Deng Yong and have no effect on Chongqing Dapeng. Fourth, Zhongbao Life's financial losses were caused by its own actions, and there is no causal relationship with the issuance of the Letter of Commitment. The court of first instance's finding on Chongqing Dapeng's liability was correct and should be upheld.

Hualong Company did not participate in the second instance proceedings and did not submit a statement.

This Court, in addition to affirming the basic facts found by the court of first instance, finds the following supplemental facts:
1. On August 15, 2003, the court of first instance interrogated Zhang Zhiyong, as recorded in an interrogation transcript. The transcript mainly includes the following points: (1) The entire RMB 90 million in funds was a financing relationship arranged between Zhongbao Life and Deng Yong, and the RMB 40 million at issue here was proactively offered by Zhongbao Life to Deng Yong after seeing that the first RMB 50 million had operated relatively well. (2) The RMB 40 million in treasury bonds was originally intended to be purchased using Zhongbao Life's own securities account (i.e., the same operational method as the first RMB 50 million), but because Zhongbao Life's securities account (account 601) had already been designated to the former Hainan Hong Kong Macao International Trust and Investment Corporation Chengdu Securities Trading Department (later renamed BOC International Securities Co., Ltd. Chengdu Renmin Zhong Road Securities Department, hereinafter "BOC International Securities"), and the designated trading could not be revoked, Zhongbao Life agreed to use Hualong Company's name (account 617) to purchase the RMB 40 million in treasury bonds. (3) The interest for the three years from 1999 to 2001 was all paid by Deng Yong to Zhongbao Life. (4) The Asset Entrusted Management Agreement and Letter of Commitment signed in the name of Chongqing Dapeng were made by Deng Yong and Zhongbao Life on their own initiative using pre-stamped blank documents to cope with inspections. (5) In November 2002, Deng Yong entrusted Attorney Chen from Hengping Law Firm to negotiate with Zhongbao Life regarding the debt issue, and Zhongbao Life requested Deng Yong to find a company with financial strength to negotiate (meaning a guarantor). In January 2003, Zhang Zhiyong was lawfully arrested for other acts unrelated to this case and lost contact with the outside world.

2. On January 10, 2003, Attorney Chen Haowen of Sichuan Hengping Law Firm issued an "Opinion Letter Regarding the Handling of Treasury Bond Funds of Zhongbao Life Insurance Company Sichuan Branch." The contents of this opinion letter are generally consistent with the situation reflected in Zhang Zhiyong's testimony: (1) In 1998, Zhongbao Life and Beihai Yinzheng Economic Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Beihai Yinzheng") consulted on financial management matters. (2) Beihai Yinzheng, following Zhongbao Life's instructions, sold two batches totaling RMB 90 million in treasury bonds for securities investment. (3) Beihai Yinzheng paid interest to Zhongbao Life for three consecutive years. (4) The securities market was relatively good at the beginning. (5) There was no written contract between the parties. (6) In November 2002, Chen Haowen negotiated with Zhongbao Life, and Zhongbao Life requested the other party to secure a guarantee from a company with financial strength. This evidence was obtained by Chengdu Dapeng from the Beihai City Public Security Bureau as new evidence before the second instance court investigation (stamped by the Public Security Bureau). Part of the opinion letter reflects statements made by "our client" (which should be legal representative Deng Yong) to Chen Haowen, and another part reflects Chen Haowen's personal experience. Upon cross-examination, Zhongbao Life did not raise any objection to the authenticity of this evidence but argued that it was new evidence and thus should not be admitted.

Furthermore, the account used by Zhongbao Life to receive interest payments from Deng Yong was still account 791293 opened at Chengdu Dapeng.

This Court, upon trial, finds: There is no dispute that Zhongbao Life transferred RMB 40 million to Chengdu Dapeng on July 26, 1999, to purchase treasury bond 000896. The main issue in this case is whether the purchase of treasury bond 000896 into Hualong Company's securities account No. 617 was Zhongbao Life's true intention. Zhongbao Life argues that account 617 was not its own Shanghai securities account; its Shanghai securities account was B880217601. Zhongbao Life did not consent to using its own funds to purchase treasury bonds for Hualong Company. Chengdu Dapeng, on the other hand, contends that it is a common practice for an investor to use its own funds to purchase securities for another's securities account. Chengdu Dapeng subordinated Hualong Company's securities account 617 under Zhongbao Life's fund account 791293 opened at Chengdu Dapeng, based on specific instructions from Zhongbao Life. The meaning of subordinating a securities account is that the owner of the fund account allows the subordinated securities account to use its funds. Subsequently, Zhongbao Life, using a trading password known only to itself, and after explicitly selecting or directly entering the number "617," purchased the treasury bonds. It then applied to revoke the designated trading of securities account 617 at Chengdu Dapeng, enabling Hualong Company to dispose of those treasury bonds at another securities company. In particular, when Zhongbao Life commissioned Chengdu Dapeng to purchase the RMB 40 million in treasury bonds, its own securities account B880217601 had already been designated at BOC International Securities. According to the rules of the Shanghai Stock Exchange, Zhongbao Life could not simultaneously use its own B880217601 securities account at Chengdu Dapeng to purchase treasury bond 000896. Under these circumstances, Zhongbao Life had to borrow another person's Shanghai securities account that were already designated at Chengdu Dapeng. The operational method of subordinating another person's securities account to purchase treasury bonds, then revoking the designated trading of that securities account to transfer the right to dispose of the treasury bonds to the other party, was a relatively common practice for capital lending or entrusted financial management at the time. Zhang Zhiyong's testimony, Chen Haowen's opinion letter, and the payment amounts and sources of over RMB 20 million in interest and proceeds all indicate that this case was not merely about purchasing treasury bonds; in reality, the purchase of treasury bonds was a means to deliver funds to Deng Yong for stock trading, with Zhongbao Life obtaining higher returns than from simple treasury bond purchases.

Whether the purchase of the RMB 40 million in treasury bond 000896 into Hualong Company's securities account 617 represented Zhongbao Life's true intention directly affects the proper evaluation of evidence such as the Application for Adding Trading Account dated July 28, 1999, and the Application for Revocation of Designated Trading dated August 10, 1999. The full title of the July 28, 1999 application is "Application for Adding/Modifying Password (for Fund/Trading Account)." Because it contains multiple options, when used, the options not involved would necessarily be deleted. Furthermore, regardless of when the title was modified, the application form objectively reflects the connection between Zhongbao Life's fund account 791293 at Chengdu Dapeng and Hualong Company's securities account 617. In securities trading practice, such a connection would indicate that funds in fund account 791293 could be used to purchase securities for securities account 617. Moreover, the "Records of Account Designation and Revocation of Designation for Shanghai Branch of China Securities Depository and Clearing Corporation Ltd." obtained by the court of first instance ex officio reflect that during the period of purchasing the RMB 40 million in treasury bonds, Zhongbao Life's own Shanghai securities account B880217601 had been designated at BOC International Securities. For Zhongbao Life to achieve its stated intention in its complaint of using its own RMB 40 million at Chengdu Dapeng to purchase treasury bond 000896, it objectively needed to use another person's Shanghai securities account already designated at Chengdu Dapeng. Additionally, Zhongbao Life had already obtained the "Triplicate Receipt for the Shareholder Chengdu Cotton and Hemp from Shanghai Securities Central Depository and Clearing Corporation" confirming that the RMB 40 million in treasury bond 000896 had been traded, indicating that Zhongbao Life already knew that the RMB 40 million in treasury bonds it had commissioned Chengdu Dapeng to purchase had actually been traded. This further confirms that Zhongbao Life had objectively used another person's Shanghai A-share account. Zhongbao Life confirmed the authenticity of the official seal on the application form but could not provide a reasonable explanation for how, during the period when its own B880217601 Shanghai A-share account was designated at another securities company, it could commission Chengdu Dapeng to purchase RMB 40 million in treasury bond 000896 without using another person's Shanghai A-share account. In fact, this would be inconsistent with the basic rules of securities trading. Therefore, it should be found that Zhongbao Life made the representation of intention to add the Shanghai securities account 617 under its fund account 791293. Although the court of first instance's finding on this point was not sufficiently precise, its conclusion that Zhongbao Life applied to subordinate account 617 is consistent with the actual circumstances of this case, and this Court affirms it.

1999年8月10日《撤销指定交易申请表》分别存在“存根联”和“客户联”，“存根联”上有“617”字样及成都大鹏经办人、部门负责人和总经理的签字，而“客户联”上没有“617”及成都大鹏经办人、复核人和负责人的签字。本院认为，撤销证券账户的指定交易意味着可能放弃对一个证券账户及所购证券的控制，中保人寿作为一个管理制度严格的金融机构，其拿回公司存档的“客户联”应当是经过交易对方签字和盖章的一联，而且“客户联”上有证券公司人员签字的三个档目；同时，空白《撤销指定交易申请表》任何一个客户都是容易取得的，因此应当认定中保人寿向法庭出示的“客户联”缺乏客观性，同时应当推定中保人寿持有经成都大鹏人员签字的“客户联”。成都大鹏认为中保人寿之所以拒不出具该客观的“客户联”原因是该联上同样也写有“617”内容，进而，能够证明“617”内容的加注是得到中保人寿认可的。根据本院《关于民事诉讼证据的若干规定》第七十五条的规定：“有证据证明一方当事人持有证据无正当理由拒不提供，如果对方当事人主张该证据的内容不利于证据持有人，可以推定该主张成立”。因此，本院推定中保人寿所持有的、真实的“客户联”上同样也写有“617”内容。另外，从该申请表的使用目的来看，其唯一用途就是撤销上海A股账户的指定交易，本该填写“证券账户：上海A股”的位置填为了“791293”，而“791293”是中保人寿在成都大鹏的资金账户，当时与该资金账户相连的只有一个上海A股账户，即为“617”，因此中保人寿的指向也应当是明确的，成都大鹏操作为撤销“617”的指定交易符合中保人寿的利益，不能认定违背了中保人寿的意思表示。中保人寿解释填写该申请表的目的是撤销其深圳证券账户，但该申请表的标题和内容仅仅涉及上海A股账户，完全不涉及深圳证券账户，而深圳证券账户不能进行撤销指定交易操作，中保人寿的解释有悖证券交易规则。因此，本院认为，填写、递交该申请表的目的是撤销已经完成以中保人寿的资金购买国债后的“617”证券账户在成都大鹏的指定交易。

同时，其后三年来中保人寿从未收到上海证券交易所派发到成都大鹏的国债利息，而由其自己向华夏证券和厦门证券的股民账户收取利息的事实也表明，中保人寿明知其在成都大鹏的4000万元资金或国债均已经不存在于成都大鹏。原审法院对张志勇所作的笔录和四川衡平律师事务所陈浩文律师《关于人寿保险公司四川分公司国债资金处理的意见函》，均分别反映了中保人寿与邓勇或其控制的华隆公司或北海银证公司之间直接存在包括本案4000万元在内的共计9000万元的资金有偿使用关系，该两份证据对这一情况的叙述互相吻合。此外，客观上三年的利息和收益也是由与邓勇控制的相关股民账户所支付。这三部分证据又与前述中保人寿增加、使用“617”证券账户及撤销“617”证券账户在成都大鹏的指定交易等一系列证据相互印证，进一步证明了使用华隆公司“617”证券账户正是中保人寿自己的行为，并非成都大鹏擅自实施的侵权行为。其后三年中，中保人寿仍使用791293资金账户接受邓勇支付利息的行为，证明与其所称当时是申请撤销该资金账户相矛盾，更进一步证明成都大鹏为中保人寿办理撤销“617”账户指定交易的行为，与中保人寿4000万元国债损失之间并无因果关系。

至于在资金账户下挂他人证券账户是否违法，这属于应当由证券监管机构处理的行政法律范畴的问题，不影响中保人寿与成都大鹏之间根据委托指定交易协议、撤销指定交易申请确认民事责任的承担，不属于本案考虑的问题。本院认为，中保人寿与成都大鹏通过签订《证券交易委托协议书》建立了委托代理法律关系，中保人寿依法应当对委托成都大鹏实施的行为承担民事责任。中保人寿将华隆公司“617”增加到其791293资金账户下购买国债，使中保人寿名下的4000万元资金变成了华隆公司名下的4000万元国债，此后中保人寿撤销“617”账户在成都大鹏的指定交易，彻底放弃了对“617”证券账户的实际控制，这正是导致华隆公司得以在厦门证券重新设定“617”账户的指定交易，并将其下挂在股民雷少成账户下作为子账户卖掉全部国债的直接原因。华隆公司未参与本案诉讼，本案中亦没有明确、充分的证据证明存在着国债处分后炒股的风险应由中保人寿自己承担的约定，原审法院判决华隆公司返还抵扣相应收益后的37831111.11元资金及相应利息正确，应予维持。华隆公司取得并能够处分本案中的4000万元国债，是中保人寿自己的行为所造成；成都大鹏并未违背中保人寿的指令，也没有实施对中保人寿的欺诈行为；其按照申请办理撤销指定交易的行为，与中保人寿的款项损失之间并不存在近因，不构成行为与损失之间的因果关系。根据《中华人民共和国民法通则》第六十三条的规定，作为代理人的成都大鹏按照中保人寿的要求实施代理行为的民事责任应当由中保人寿承担。

此外，重庆大鹏与中保人寿签订资产委托管理协议书时中保人寿在成都大鹏的国债早已被华隆公司指定到了厦门证券并被变卖，中保人寿自始未将协议书中所约定的000896国债实际交付给重庆大鹏，且488万元高额收益也并非重庆大鹏直接支付，亦没有证据证明系他人代重庆大鹏支付，故该份协议书应认定为并未实际履行。2002年3月重庆大鹏向中保人寿出具承诺书时，中保人寿的资金亦早已被华隆公司所占用，故该承诺书与中保人寿的经济损失之间亦并无直接因果关系，重庆大鹏对中保人寿的损失不应承担责任。

综上，成都大鹏关于不构成侵权的上诉理由成立，本院予以支持。原审法院关于成都大鹏擅自撤销617账户指定交易的事实认定不当，判决成都大鹏承担中保人寿损失总额90%的赔偿责任，属于适用法律司对大鹏证券有限责任公司成都锣锅巷证错误，应予纠正。中保人寿要求判定重庆大券营业部的诉讼请求。鹏承担赔偿责任的上诉理由不成立，本院四、驳回中国人寿保险公司成都分公予以驳回。原审法院认定重庆大鹏不承担司对大鹏证券有限责任公司重庆陕西路证赔偿责任正确，但在判决主文中未作表述券交易营业部的诉讼请求。不当，应予以纠正。原审法院判决华隆公司本案一审案件受理费252010元，由承担赔偿责任正确，本院予以维持；华隆公四川省华隆投资顾问有限公司承担司不能偿还的部分，因系由中保人寿撤销126005元，中国人寿保险公司成都分公司指定交易而将4000万元交由华隆公司使承担126005元。二审案件受理费252010用，并从中得到三年的国债利息，中保人寿元，由中国人寿保险公司成都分公司承担。亦有过错，对于该损失应当自行承担。本院本判决为终审判决。根据《中华人民共和国民法通则》第六十三条，第一百一十七条第一款、第三款，《中华人民共和国民事诉讼法》第一百五十三条第一款第（一）、（二）、（三）项及第一百五十八条之规定，判决如下：

一、维持四川省高级人民法院（2003）川民初字第22号民事判决书主文第一项。

二、撤销上述民事判决主文第二项。

三、驳回中国人寿保险公司成都分公司对大鹏证券有限责任公司成都锣锅巷证券营业部的诉讼请求。

四、驳回中国人寿保险公司成都分公司对大鹏证券有限责任公司重庆陕西路证券交易营业部的诉讼请求。

本案一审案件受理费252010元，由四川省华隆投资顾问有限公司承担126005元，中国人寿保险公司成都分公司承担126005元。二审案件受理费252010元，由中国人寿保险公司成都分公司承担。

本判决为终审判决。

审　判　长　　吴庆宝

代理审判员　　宫邦友

代理审判员　　刘　敏

二〇〇五年一月十日

书　记　员　　孔　玲

［审判长简介］

吴庆宝高级法官：1964年出生，法学学士，2001年起任最高人民法院审判员。

The Application for Revocation of Designated Transaction dated August 10, 1999 consisted of a "Counterfoil" and a "Customer Copy." The "Counterfoil" bore the notation "617" and the signatures of the Chengdu Dapeng handling person, department head, and general manager, whereas the "Customer Copy" did not bear the notation "617" or the signatures of the Chengdu Dapeng handling person, reviewer, and responsible person. This Court is of the opinion that revoking the designated transaction of a securities account implies the potential relinquishment of control over that securities account and the securities purchased therein. As a financial institution with strict management systems, the "Customer Copy" retained by China Life for its archives should have been the copy signed and sealed by the counterparty, and should have contained three columns signed by personnel of the securities company. Furthermore, blank copies of the Application for Revocation of Designated Transaction are readily obtainable by any customer. Therefore, it should be determined that the "Customer Copy" presented by China Life to the court lacks objectivity, and it should be inferred that China Life holds a "Customer Copy" that bears the signatures of Chengdu Dapeng personnel. Chengdu Dapeng contends that the reason China Life refuses to produce this objective "Customer Copy" is because that copy also contains the notation "617," which would prove that the addition of the "617" notation was approved by China Life. Pursuant to Article 75 of the "Several Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Evidence in Civil Proceedings": "If there is evidence that a party holds evidence and, without justifiable reasons, refuses to provide it, and the opposing party claims that the content of the evidence is unfavorable to the holder, it may be inferred that the opposing party's claim is established." Accordingly, this Court infers that the genuine "Customer Copy" held by China Life also contains the notation "617." Moreover, considering the purpose of the application form, its sole use was to revoke the designated transaction of a Shanghai A-share account. The space that should have been filled in with "Securities Account: Shanghai A-Share" was instead filled in with "791293," which was China Life's capital account at Chengdu Dapeng. At that time, only one Shanghai A-share account was linked to that capital account, namely "617." Therefore, China Life's intent was clear, and Chengdu Dapeng's action of revoking the designated transaction for "617" was in line with China Life's interests and cannot be deemed contrary to China Life's intention. China Life explained that the purpose of filling out the application form was to cancel its Shenzhen securities account. However, the title and content of the application form solely pertained to Shanghai A-share accounts and did not concern Shenzhen securities accounts at all. Furthermore, a Shenzhen securities account cannot be subject to a revocation of designated transaction operation. China Life's explanation contradicts securities trading rules. Therefore, this Court holds that the purpose of filling out and submitting the application form was to revoke the designated transaction of the "617" securities account at Chengdu Dapeng, which had already been used to purchase treasury bonds with China Life's funds.

Meanwhile, for three years thereafter, China Life never received the interest on treasury bonds distributed by the Shanghai Stock Exchange to Chengdu Dapeng. The fact that China Life instead collected interest from the shareholder accounts at Huaxia Securities and Xiamen Securities also indicates that China Life was fully aware that its RMB 40 million in funds or treasury bonds at Chengdu Dapeng were no longer with Chengdu Dapeng. The record of the interview with Zhang Zhiyong made by the court of first instance and the "Opinion Letter Regarding the Handling of Treasury Bond Funds of the Sichuan Branch of Life Insurance Company" by Attorney Chen Haowen of Sichuan Hengping Law Firm, both reflect a direct, for-value fund utilization relationship between China Life and Deng Yong or his controlled Hualong Company or Beihai Yinzheng Company, involving a total of RMB 90 million, including the RMB 40 million in this case. The two pieces of evidence are consistent in their description of this situation. Additionally, the objectively received interest and gains over the three years were paid by the relevant shareholder accounts controlled by Deng Yong. These three pieces of evidence, in conjunction with the series of evidence mentioned above concerning China Life's addition and use of the "617" securities account and the revocation of the designated transaction of the "617" securities account at Chengdu Dapeng, mutually corroborate each other, further proving that the use of Hualong Company's "617" securities account was China Life's own act, not an unauthorized tort by Chengdu Dapeng. The fact that China Life continued to use capital account 791293 to receive interest payments from Deng Yong over the following three years contradicts its claim that it was then applying to revoke that capital account, and further proves that Chengdu Dapeng's act of handling the revocation of the designated transaction for the "617" account bears no causal relationship with the loss of China Life's RMB 40 million in treasury bonds.

As for whether linking another person's securities account under a capital account is illegal, this is a matter falling within the administrative legal sphere to be handled by securities regulatory authorities. It does not affect the determination of civil liability between China Life and Chengdu Dapeng under the designated transaction agency agreement and the application for revocation of designated transaction, and is not an issue to be considered in this case. This Court holds that China Life and Chengdu Dapeng established a principal-agent legal relationship by entering into the "Securities Trading Agency Agreement." China Life shall bear civil liability for the acts performed by Chengdu Dapeng as its agent, in accordance with the law. By adding Hualong Company's "617" account under its 791293 capital account to purchase treasury bonds, China Life converted the RMB 40 million in funds under its name into RMB 40 million in treasury bonds under Hualong Company's name. Subsequently, China Life revoked the designated transaction of the "617" account at Chengdu Dapeng, completely relinquishing actual control over the "617" securities account. This was the direct cause that enabled Hualong Company to re-establish a designated transaction for the "617" account at Xiamen Securities and link it as a sub-account under the shareholder Lei Shaocheng's account, thereby selling all the treasury bonds. Hualong Company did not participate in the litigation of this case, and there is no clear and sufficient evidence in this case to prove the existence of an agreement that the risk of stock trading after the disposal of the treasury bonds should be borne by China Life itself. The judgment of the court of first instance ordering Hualong Company to return RMB 37,831,111.11 after deducting corresponding gains, plus corresponding interest, is correct and should be affirmed. The fact that Hualong Company obtained and was able to dispose of the RMB 40 million in treasury bonds in this case was caused by China Life's own acts. Chengdu Dapeng did not violate China Life's instructions, nor did it commit any fraud against China Life. There is no proximate cause between its act of handling the revocation of designated transaction upon application and the loss of China Life's funds; a causal relationship between the act and the loss is not established. Pursuant to Article 63 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, Chengdu Dapeng, as the agent, performed the agency act in accordance with China Life's requirements, and the civil liability arising therefrom shall be borne by China Life.

Furthermore, when Chongqing Dapeng and China Life entered into the Asset Entrusted Management Agreement, the treasury bonds of China Life held at Chengdu Dapeng had already been designated by Hualong Company to Xiamen Securities and sold. China Life had never actually delivered the treasury bonds numbered 000896 as stipulated in the agreement to Chongqing Dapeng. Moreover, the high returns of RMB 4.88 million were not directly paid by Chongqing Dapeng, and there is no evidence that they were paid by another party on behalf of Chongqing Dapeng. Therefore, this agreement should be deemed as not having been actually performed. When Chongqing Dapeng issued a letter of commitment to China Life in March 2002, China Life's funds had already been occupied by Hualong Company. Therefore, there is no direct causal relationship between this letter of commitment and China Life's economic losses. Chongqing Dapeng shall not be liable for China Life's losses.

In summary, Chengdu Dapeng's ground of appeal that it did not constitute a tort is established and is supported by this Court. The court of first instance's incorrect determination of the facts that Chengdu Dapeng unilaterally revoked the designated transaction for the 617 account, and its judgment ordering Chengdu Dapeng to bear 90% of China Life's total losses, constitutes an error in the application of law and should be corrected. China Life's ground of appeal requesting that Chongqing Dapeng be held liable for compensation is not established, and is hereby dismissed. The court of first instance's determination that Chongqing Dapeng is not liable for compensation is correct, but the failure to state this in the main text of the judgment was improper and should be corrected. The court of first instance's judgment that Hualong Company is liable for compensation is correct and is affirmed by this Court. Regarding the portion of the liability that Hualong Company is unable to satisfy, since it was China Life's revocation of the designated transaction that placed the RMB 40 million under Hualong Company's use, from which China Life received three years of treasury bond interest, China Life is also at fault and shall bear this loss itself. Pursuant to Article 63, Article 117, paragraphs 1 and 3 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 153, paragraph 1, subparagraphs (1), (2), and (3) and Article 158 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the judgment is as follows:

1. Affirm item 1 of the main text of the Civil Judgment (2003) Chuan Chu Zi No. 22 of the Sichuan High People's Court.

2. Reverse item 2 of the said civil judgment.

3. Dismiss the claims of China Life Insurance Company Chengdu Branch against the Chengdu Luoguo Lane Securities Business Department of Dapeng Securities Co., Ltd.

4. Dismiss the claims of China Life Insurance Company Chengdu Branch against the Chongqing Shaanxi Road Securities Trading Business Department of Dapeng Securities Co., Ltd.

The court acceptance fee for the first instance is RMB 252,010, of which Sichuan Hualong Investment Consulting Co., Ltd. shall bear RMB 126,005, and China Life Insurance Company Chengdu Branch shall bear RMB 126,005. The court acceptance fee for the second instance is RMB 252,010, to be borne by China Life Insurance Company Chengdu Branch.

This judgment is final.
